stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 33 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 32+1 weeks presents with a painless bright red vaginal bleed that soaked a pad over the last hour. She has had two prior lower segment caesarean sections.

Her morphology scan at 20 weeks and repeat scan at 28 weeks showed a placenta covering the internal cervical os (grade 4). She has been abstaining from intercourse and vaginal examinations since. She has known blood group O negative.

On assessment she looks alert with warm peripheries. Abdomen is soft and non tender; presenting part is high and mobile. Speculum examination is deferred. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140, moderate variability, accelerations, and no decelerations.

Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8. Ongoing bleeding is estimated at 250 mL over the last 30 minutes. Two large bore intravenous cannulas are sited, full blood count, group and hold, and coagulation are drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/64, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Blood loss: 250 mL ongoing over 30 minutes; bright red painless
data_table.Foetal CTG: Baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Prior imaging: 20 and 28 week scans: placenta covering internal os (grade 4)
data_table.Obstetric history: Two prior lower segment caesareans; group O negative
data_table.Access: Two large bore IV cannulas; FBC, group and hold, coags drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give IM betamethasone 11.4 mg, cross match blood, Anti D 625 IU, and prepare for possible category one caesarean
options.rationale: At 32+1 weeks with a grade 4 praevia and ongoing bleed, RANZCOG recommends corticosteroids for lung maturity, cross matched blood, Anti D for a Rh negative woman, and prompt caesarean if maternal or foetal compromise occurs (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Proceed to a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and confirm the source of bleeding before any imaging
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in known or suspected placenta praevia because it can precipitate massive haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery with a controlled artificial rupture of membranes to compress the placental edge
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is not appropriate in grade 4 praevia because the placenta covers the internal os; caesarean is mandatory for these women (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient follow up in the antenatal clinic in 48 hours once the bright red bleeding has slowed
options.rationale: Any antepartum haemorrhage at this gestation with grade 4 praevia mandates inpatient admission for surveillance because rebleeding is common (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and defer betamethasone corticosteroids until the visible bleeding has settled
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid can be considered as an adjunct in antepartum haemorrhage but does not replace corticosteroids, which should be given without delay at this preterm gestation (Source: RANZCOG Placenta praevia and accreta).

explanation.summary: This is a preterm bleed with a grade 4 placenta praevia at 32+1 weeks. Priorities are corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity, Anti D for a Rh negative woman, cross matched blood, and readiness for category one caesarean if maternal or foetal compromise develops. Digital vaginal examination and any attempt at vaginal delivery are contraindicated.
key_points: No digital vaginal examination in praevia.
Grade 4 praevia is a caesarean delivery.
Give betamethasone, cross match, and Anti D 625 IU if Rh negative.
explanation.pearls: In known grade 4 placenta praevia bleeding at 32 weeks, give betamethasone, cross match blood, Anti D if Rh negative, and prepare for category one caesarean; digital vaginal examination is forbidden.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit. A 32 year old primigravida at 36+5 weeks has a persistent frank breech presentation on ultrasound today after an unsuccessful external cephalic version 2 hours ago.

Estimated foetal weight is 3.2 kg with an amniotic fluid index of 12 cm and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. She has no cephalopelvic disproportion on examination and no hyperextension of the foetal neck. She has had no antepartum complications.

She asks about mode of birth. She has read that vaginal breech birth can be attempted at experienced units and wants an honest discussion. Her partner is supportive of either option. The senior obstetrician has agreed to be available.

data_table.Foetal parameters: Frank breech; EFW 3.2 kg; AFI 12 cm; UA Doppler within normal limits; no neck hyperextension
data_table.Maternal: 36+5 weeks; primigravida; no obstetric complications; adequate maternal pelvis on examination
data_table.Care: Senior obstetric team on call; woman wants an evidence based discussion

lead_in: What information best reflects the evidence base to guide her decision?

options.text: Planned vaginal breech birth has equivalent or lower perinatal morbidity than caesarean section in selected primigravidae
options.rationale: Contemporary meta-analyses of selected planned vaginal breech births at experienced units suggest closer outcomes than the Term Breech Trial but do not show lower morbidity than planned caesarean (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: Planned caesarean has a lower composite of perinatal mortality and serious morbidity than planned vaginal breech
options.rationale: The Term Breech Trial and subsequent RANZCOG position support planned caesarean as lower risk for the composite of perinatal death and serious neonatal morbidity in singleton term breech; long term outcomes at 2 years show no difference (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: Planned caesarean increases the risk of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage relative to a planned vaginal breech birth
options.rationale: Planned caesarean reduces, not increases, the risk of intracranial haemorrhage and other serious neonatal morbidity in term breech (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

options.text: A trial of vaginal breech is only reasonable if a second attempt at external cephalic version fails at 39 weeks under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: A second ECV attempt is not mandated by Australian pathways; the discussion at this gestation is between planned caesarean and planned vaginal breech at experienced units (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version).

options.text: Estimated foetal weight above 3 kg alone contraindicates any attempt at planned vaginal breech birth at term
options.rationale: Australian units typically consider EFW between 2.5 and 4 kg for planned vaginal breech; 3.2 kg is not itself a contraindication (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term

explanation.summary: For singleton term breech, the Term Breech Trial and RANZCOG position support planned caesarean as lower risk than planned vaginal breech for the composite of perinatal death and serious neonatal morbidity. Long term outcomes at 2 years are similar. Vaginal breech remains an option at experienced units after careful counselling and case selection.
key_points: Planned caesarean reduces perinatal composite risk versus planned vaginal breech.
EFW between 2.5 and 4 kg and no neck hyperextension are typical selection criteria.
Long term outcomes at 2 years are similar.
explanation.pearls: Evidence based counselling for term breech at Australian units: planned caesarean lowers perinatal composite risk relative to planned vaginal breech, with equivalent long term outcomes at 2 years.

sources.label: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation at Term
Term Breech Trial (Hannah et al. Lancet 2000)

stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has agreed to commence lithium after two manic episodes in 18 months.

She was well between episodes, has no known other medical conditions, uses combined oral contraceptive pills, and does not use alcohol or recreational substances. She works as a childcare educator, drinks 2 to 3 L of water per day, and drives a car.

Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. There is no goitre, no tremor, and no oedema on examination. She is normotensive.

She asks what tests she needs before starting lithium and how monitoring will occur once she is on treatment.

data_table.Diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder; two manic episodes in 18 months
data_table.Comorbidities: Nil; no substance use; no chronic medical illness
data_table.Examination: BMI 24 kg/m2; no goitre, tremor or oedema; normotensive

lead_in: Which baseline workup best matches Australian practice before starting lithium?

options.text: Genetic HLA-B*1502 testing, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function, and 12 lead ECG before starting the drug
options.rationale: HLA-B*1502 is relevant to carbamazepine and phenytoin in Han Chinese and related ancestries, not to lithium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Urea and electrolytes and thyroid function only, with lithium level checked once monthly after starting
options.rationale: Baseline monitoring must also cover calcium and PTH given hyperparathyroidism risk, an ECG for conduction, and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive potential; monthly lithium levels alone are insufficient early in titration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: UEC, thyroid function, calcium and PTH, full blood count, ECG, urinalysis, and serum beta hCG at baseline
options.rationale: eTG and RANZCP recommend baseline UEC, TFTs, calcium and PTH, FBC, ECG, and urinalysis before lithium, with a serum beta hCG in women of reproductive potential because of first trimester Ebstein anomaly risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: 24 hour urine collection for creatinine clearance, full blood count, and LFTs without electrolytes or thyroid
options.rationale: A 24 hour urine collection is not required routinely; eGFR from serum creatinine is adequate at baseline and liver function tests are not part of the lithium panel (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Baseline HbA1c and lipid panel alone because lithium is associated with metabolic syndrome and weight gain
options.rationale: Metabolic monitoring is a priority for second generation antipsychotics rather than lithium; HbA1c and lipids are not the required baseline for lithium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Lithium baseline in Australia includes renal (UEC), thyroid (TFT), parathyroid (calcium and PTH), full blood count, ECG, urinalysis, and beta hCG in women of reproductive potential. Ongoing monitoring includes 12 hour post dose lithium levels every 3 months and TFT, UEC, calcium every 6 months long term. HbA1c and lipid panels drive antipsychotic metabolic monitoring rather than the lithium baseline.
key_points: Include calcium and PTH at baseline for lithium.
ECG is part of the baseline lithium panel.
Serum beta hCG matters in women of reproductive potential before initiation.
explanation.pearls: Lithium baseline in Australian practice includes calcium and PTH alongside UEC, TFT, FBC, ECG, and urinalysis, plus a serum beta hCG in women of reproductive potential.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD stimulant initiation and driving
stem:
You are the general adult psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old man with a new diagnosis of adult ADHD, combined presentation, made after structured assessment including collateral from parents and school reports.

He is fit and well, has no personal or family history of stroke or cardiac disease, and drinks 6 standard drinks per week. He denies stimulant misuse and has never used methamphetamine.

Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular, ECG shows sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation. He has a full unrestricted driver licence and works as a solicitor. He asks specifically about starting medication and whether it will affect his driving.

data_table.Diagnosis: Adult ADHD combined presentation; collateral corroborated
data_table.Medical: No cardiac disease; no personal or family history of stroke
data_table.Substance use: 6 standard drinks weekly; denies stimulant misuse; no methamphetamine
data_table.Cardiovascular: BP 128/78; ECG sinus rhythm; no QT prolongation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy and driving advice?

options.text: Commence modafinil 100 mg orally daily because it is a Schedule 4 stimulant analogue with a favourable cardiac profile
options.rationale: Modafinil is not TGA approved for ADHD and is not first line under RANZCP guidance (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily because non stimulant medication avoids any need for licence notification
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a second line non stimulant option rather than first line for typical adult ADHD; licence notification is still required for treated ADHD irrespective of drug class (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily to address inattention through mood improvement rather than direct effect
options.rationale: SSRIs are not a treatment for core ADHD inattention and hyperactivity, though they treat comorbid anxiety or depression (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, and notify the licensing authority for a conditional licence
options.rationale: Australian guidance supports methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine as first line for adult ADHD; Assessing Fitness to Drive requires reporting to the licensing authority for a conditional licence review when treated ADHD is medically managed (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline; Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022).

options.text: Trial cognitive behavioural therapy for ADHD as sole treatment for 12 months before considering any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: CBT for ADHD is a valuable adjunct but delaying pharmacotherapy 12 months in a functionally impaired adult is not aligned with Australian guidance (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

explanation.summary: First line adult ADHD pharmacotherapy in Australia is a stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate. Atomoxetine is a second line non stimulant option and modafinil is not TGA approved for ADHD. Treated ADHD is notifiable to the driver licensing authority under Assessing Fitness to Drive for review of a conditional licence, irrespective of drug class.
key_points: Lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate is first line adult ADHD pharmacotherapy.
Atomoxetine is second line non stimulant.
AFTD requires driver licence authority notification for treated ADHD.
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD treated with pharmacotherapy is notifiable under Assessing Fitness to Drive regardless of whether the drug is a stimulant or atomoxetine.

subtopic_detail: EPDS interpretation with active suicidal ideation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 30 year old woman for her 6 week postnatal check. She lives with her partner and their first baby, who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal birth.

She reports she is exhausted and tearful most days but says she is coping. On completion of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale in the waiting room she scores 16, and item 10 (the self harm item) is answered as sometimes.

She takes no regular medications and has no personal history of psychiatric illness. Her mother had postnatal depression treated by her general practitioner. She is breastfeeding her baby without difficulty.

data_table.History: Nil past psychiatric history; mother had postnatal depression
data_table.Support: Partner and grandparents involved; baby breastfeeding well; term vaginal birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Advise her to wean the baby from breastfeeding first before any mental health intervention or medication
options.rationale: Weaning is not required to commence psychological or pharmacological treatment; several antidepressants including sertraline are compatible with breastfeeding (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily immediately because sertraline has the lowest breast milk transfer among SSRIs
options.rationale: SSRI initiation may be appropriate later but does not replace risk assessment; medication should not be started before quantifying suicidal thoughts and safety planning (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.text: Reassure her that scores under 20 are consistent with the baby blues and rescreen with EPDS at 3 months
options.rationale: An EPDS of 13 or above suggests probable depression and a positive item 10 requires immediate risk assessment, not deferred rescreening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.text: Refer to the perinatal psychiatry outpatient clinic in 4 weeks time without any further assessment today
options.rationale: A 4 week wait without present day risk assessment leaves an at risk mother without immediate safety planning (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.text: Undertake a structured suicide risk assessment now, including detail of self harm thoughts, before treatment
options.rationale: Any positive answer on EPDS item 10 mandates a face to face risk assessment with detail of frequency, intent, plan, and access to means before any prescription or referral decision (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

explanation.summary: An EPDS of 16 with a positive item 10 requires immediate structured suicide risk assessment before treatment decisions. Treatment options and referral pathways follow that assessment. Weaning breastfeeding is not required to start compatible antidepressants.
key_points: EPDS 13 or above suggests probable depression.
Any positive item 10 mandates immediate risk assessment.
Sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding when treatment is warranted.
explanation.pearls: A positive EPDS item 10 answered other than 'never' triggers same day structured suicide risk assessment before pharmacotherapy or referral is decided.

sources.label: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline
